summary: Venezuela admits citizens of the EU, the United Kingdom and most of Latin America visa-free for up to 90 days, while United States passport holders need a visa that has been very difficult to obtain since consular relations were suspended in 2019, and several governments, including the United States, advise against all travel to the country.

vaccinations.text: Not generally demanded on arrival, but Venezuela has yellow fever risk areas south and east of the Orinoco, so vaccination is recommended, and Brazil, Colombia and several Caribbean states require the certificate from travelers arriving from Venezuela.

vaccinations.name: Malaria prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: Not an entry requirement. Malaria transmission has risen sharply in Bolívar and Amazonas states and in the mining areas, and diagnosis and treatment are hard to obtain locally. Take advice from a travel clinic before any trip outside the main cities.

source.name: Ministerio del Poder Popular para Relaciones Exteriores — Venezuela

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not an entry requirement, but it matters more here than almost anywhere: hospitals face shortages of medicines and equipment, most travel policies exclude countries under a do-not-travel advisory, and evacuation coverage has to be arranged specifically. Read the exclusions before you rely on a policy.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Venezuela Travel Advisory

onwardTicket.text: Visa-free visitors are admitted on the basis of a confirmed return or onward ticket within the permitted stay, and airlines check it at boarding. The officer writes the number of days granted on the entry stamp. It is often fewer than 90.

source.name: Ministerio del Poder Popular para Relaciones Exteriores — Venezuela

proofOfFunds.text: No published amount, but officers may ask how you will pay for your stay and where you are staying. In practice visitors need US dollars in cash, since foreign cards mostly do not work.

source.name: Ministerio del Poder Popular para Relaciones Exteriores — Venezuela

currencyLimits.text: Cash of USD 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure. Exchange controls have been loosened but the rules change often. Declare what you carry and keep the form, because you may be asked for it on the way out.

source.name: SENIAT — Venezuelan customs and tax authority

notes: Drone equipment, satellite phones and professional camera gear draw scrutiny; journalists have been detained for filming without accreditation.
Airport departure taxes and fees are sometimes demanded in cash at the counter even when they are supposed to be included in the ticket.
Do not photograph airports, military installations, police or protests — cameras and phones have been confiscated.

payments.text: The economy is heavily dollarised after years of hyperinflation: US dollars in cash are accepted — and often preferred — for hotels, meals and taxis, while the bolívar loses value quickly and is used mainly for small change. Foreign cards are usually declined and international ATM withdrawals rarely work, so bring enough clean, small-denomination US notes for the whole trip.

safety.text: Venezuela is one of the most dangerous countries in the hemisphere for visitors. Violent crime, armed robbery and express kidnapping are common in Caracas and other cities; there is a real risk of wrongful detention of foreign nationals; power cuts, fuel and medicine shortages are routine; and the Colombian border states are affected by armed groups. The United States and several other governments advise against all travel, and consular help for travelers in trouble is extremely limited.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Venezuela Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is the dry season, the practical window for Los Roques, Mérida and the Gran Sabana. Angel Falls is the exception. The boat trip up the Churún river needs the high water of the June-to-November wet season.

idp.text: Venezuela is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

tips.text: Check your own government's advice before doing anything else. The United States advises against all travel to Venezuela and has no embassy operating in Caracas; several European governments advise against all nonessential travel. Travel insurance is normally void for a destination under a do-not-travel advisory.

Venezuelan consular services in the United States have been suspended since 2019 and the US embassy in Caracas suspended operations in the same year. US citizens who need a Venezuelan visa must apply through a Venezuelan consulate in a third country, and there is no US consular assistance available inside Venezuela if something goes wrong.

Bring US dollars in cash — small, clean, undamaged notes. Foreign cards are generally refused, ATMs seldom pay out to international cards, and torn or marked bills are rejected. Do not rely on being able to get money once you are in the country.

Visa-free entry is not automatic for the full 90 days: the officer writes the number of days granted on the stamp, sometimes far fewer. Check it at the desk, because overstaying means fines and problems at departure.

Land borders with Colombia and Brazil open and close at short notice and the surrounding states are affected by armed groups and smuggling. If you must travel overland, check the crossing's status the same week and never move at night.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Venezuela?
faq.answer: It depends on your passport. Citizens of the EU and EEA, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Canada and most Latin American and Caribbean countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days for tourism, with a confirmed onward ticket. United States passport holders need a visa, and so does everyone not on the exemption list — applications go through a Venezuelan embassy or consulate, and processing is slow and unpredictable.

faq.question: Can US citizens travel to Venezuela?
faq.answer: It is legally possible but practically very difficult, and the US government advises against all travel. A visa is required, Venezuelan consulates in the United States have been closed since 2019, so applications must be made through a Venezuelan consulate in another country, and the US embassy in Caracas is not operating — meaning no consular assistance if you are detained, robbed or hospitalised. US nationals have been wrongfully detained in Venezuela. Confirm the current position with the Venezuelan Ministry of Foreign Affairs before making any plans.

faq.question: How long can visa-free visitors stay in Venezuela?
faq.answer: Up to 90 days per entry in principle, but the officer at the border writes the actual number of days on the stamp and often grants fewer. Extensions can be requested from the immigration authority (SAIME) inside the country, though the process is slow. Check your stamp before leaving the counter.

faq.question: What money should I take to Venezuela?
faq.answer: US dollars in cash. Years of hyperinflation have left the economy largely dollarised: hotels, restaurants and taxis quote and accept dollars, while the bolívar is used for small change. Foreign cards are usually declined and international ATM withdrawals rarely work, so bring small, clean notes covering the whole trip.

faq.question: Is Venezuela safe to visit?
faq.answer: No, not by ordinary standards. Violent crime, armed robbery and express kidnapping are common in the cities, wrongful detention of foreigners is a documented risk, medicine and fuel shortages and long power cuts are routine, and the Colombian border states are contested by armed groups. Several governments advise against all travel, and most travel insurance will not cover you there.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Venezuela?
faq.answer: It is not usually demanded on entry, but Venezuela has yellow fever risk areas south and east of the Orinoco, so vaccination is recommended. It also matters on the way out: Brazil, Colombia and several Caribbean countries ask travelers arriving from Venezuela for the certificate.
